newsitem.title: USA: Dlr holds early gains into U.S. close, up slightly.
newsitem.headline: Dlr holds early gains into U.S. close, up slightly.

text.p: The dollar held its overnight gains in U.S. trade, closing nearly flat after holding off profit-takers, dealers and analysts said.
The greenback saw steady bid interest after a surprising Swiss interest rate cut and signs of Italian economic vigor.
Switzerland cut its discount rate to an 18-year low at 1.0 percent from 1.5 and investors fled Swiss francs and marks.

"People understood Switzerland had to do something to get its economy going. I don't think they were quite ready to see such a large reduction in rates," said Lisa Finstrom, currency analyst at Smith Barney.
The dollar edged higher to close at 1.2542/47 Swiss francs from 1.2525/35 at the open, but up sharply from 1.2410/20 at Wednesday's close.
The dollar was also barely higher at 110.62/72 yen from 110.60/65 and 1.5234/39 marks from 1.5227/30 at the open, but held most of a rise from 1.5165/75 marks at Wednesday's close.
The dollar/Swiss rally also hurt the mark, with investors also expecting lower German interest rates in coming months.
"People that had been flocking to the Swiss francs got hurt a bit and the higher dollar puts pressure on the mark," said Gabriel Grippo, chief currency dealer at Credit Agricole.

The lira saw solid buying for a second straight day, boosted by official Italian predictions that Italy would slash its budget deficit to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product in 1997, qualifying for a proposed single European currency.
The lira remained near its strongest level in two years, reached Wednesday, below 1000 to the mark. Mark/lira sales also bolstered the dollar against the mark, dealers said.
"There was more talk about Italy doing well. That should continue to put pressure on the mark and put legs under the dollar," Grippo said.
Much of the dollar's rally occurred in Asian and European trading. As markets closed in Europe, many investors sold off dollars to take profits, limiting further dollar gains.

But an afternoon report that Japanese Ministry of Finance official Eisuke Sakakibara called the United States the best place for Japanese investment helped the dollar edge to a new session high against the yen, dealers said.

Meanwhile, influential economist Fred Bergsten, director of the Institute for International Economics, told reporters in Washington that Japanese officials were seeking to weaken the yen to lower the cost of Japanese exports.
"The dollar has to play some catch-up against the yen," said Grippo. "I think tomorrow we should take out 111 (yen) and test 111.50."
The dollar's 1996 high is 111.19 yen reached on July 8.
Investors appear to have already forgotten their disappointment at Federal Reserve officials' decision not to raise interest rates at a policy making meeting Tuesday.

A report of a surprising 3.1-percent drop in durable goods orders in August eased investor fear that the U.S. economy may overheat and see higher inflation. That stoked a sharp rally in Treasury bond prices and lifted the dollar, dealers said.
"There was a little nervousness about how prudent that Fed decision will prove to be, but now there's a perception that our long-term interest rates aren't looking so fearful," Finstrom said.

In other trade, sterling inched higher to $1.5612/17 from $1.5608/18 at the open. The dollar slipped to Canadian $1.3676/81 from C$1.3678/83. The Australian dollar hardly moved, closing at $0.7925/30 from $0.7924/29.
--Chris Stetkiewicz, 212-859-1664
